body: On the kaval, a Balkan rim-blown flute, blow too hard and the note doesn't rise smoothly - it jumps straight to the next harmonic, cracking at the break.
A scooped EQ cuts the mids while boosting lows and highs, drawing a curve that literally smiles up at both ends - the classic scooped-mid metal guitar tone.
A snow avalanche booms in infrasound too low to hear - sensors kilometres away can detect and time it in total darkness or blinding snow.
A white label is a vinyl single with a deliberately blank centre label - sent early to DJs to test a track, or used to hide who made an unofficial release.
Acoustophoresis uses standing sound waves like sonic tweezers, nudging suspended cells to pressure nodes so they can be sorted without ever being touched.
Old tape can get 'sticky-shed syndrome' as its glue absorbs moisture and turns gummy - gentle baking can dry it out for one last safe transfer.
At Epidaurus the stone seat rows act as a filter, cutting low background rumble while passing a voice's higher tones clear to the back row.
The free span of tape between guides can vibrate lengthwise like a plucked string - the hidden cause of the high-pitched warble called scrape flutter.
A masking line is traced from a theatre's most extreme seat, not the best one - curtains hiding the wings must block the view from the worst angle in the house.
Vinyl mastering forces a running order: sound quality degrades toward the record's center, so the gentlest, quietest song often goes last on a side.
Record a wave, flip it in time, and play it back: it retraces its path and refocuses on the source - scattering along the way actually sharpens the focus.
Before oscilloscopes went digital, an X-Y recorder drew graphs the old way: a pen physically tracing one measured value against another straight onto paper.
A supersonic jet can lock into a feedback loop with itself - shockwaves kick off waves that circle back and reinforce, loud enough to crack nearby metal.
Early capacitors used paper soaked in wax or oil as the insulator, rolled between metal foils - a construction almost entirely replaced by plastic film.
A small beeper clipped to fishing nets to warn dolphins and porpoises away - quieter than a scare device, it just lets them know the net is there.
A "phone jack" carries its name from the earliest telephone switchboards - the quarter-inch socket outlived the switchboards by a century and kept the name.
Idiophone: an instrument that sounds from its own rigid body vibrating, no strings or drumskin needed - rattles, bells and clappers all qualify.
Feedback squeal has a proper, lesser-known name: the Larsen effect, honoring physicist Søren Larsen behind that recirculating microphone-to-speaker howl.
The jansky measures how strong a radio signal from space is - power per square meter per hertz, named for Karl Jansky, who first detected cosmic radio noise.
Tube mics can't run on standard 48V phantom power - the valve needs its own heater and plate voltages, so it ships with a dedicated power supply and cable.
The T phase is a seismic signal that spends most of its trip as sound in the ocean at just 1.5 km/s - so slow it arrives third, behind the true seismic waves.
Impulse time-weighting on old sound meters jumped fast and eased back slowly to catch sharp bangs - now dropped from the standard, kept only as a footnote.
Railway rails ring near 1 kHz, staying still at each sleeper and bulging in between - the same resonance that carves corrugation into the rail head.
The proscenium, theatre's picture-frame opening onto the stage, borrows its name from the Greek proskenion - which actually named a different part entirely.
Photothermal acoustic detection turns absorbed light directly into sound: a sample warms a hair, expands, and quite literally sings back to the detector.
Flanging got its name literally: engineers made the sweeping effect by pressing a finger on a tape reel's flange to drag one of two synced copies out of time.
Archaeologists measure a cave's reverberation by popping a balloon in it - a cheap, loud, briefly useful stand-in for proper test equipment.
Tape can curl sideways into a shallow trough as its coating shrinks faster than its backing, lifting the edges away from the head it needs to touch.
Acoustic microscopy scales ultrasound up to billions of cycles per second, letting sound reveal cracks and voids inside a material at near-optical resolution.
Before digital reverb, studios built a hard-walled room, played a speaker into it, and re-recorded the bouncing echoes with a microphone.
Sliding a finger along a gut or nylon string glides the pitch smoothly, with no break - the same trick a trombone slide does, on a string instead of a tube.
A mule block is a pulley that just turns a rigging line around a corner - it redirects the rope but, unlike the lifting blocks, carries none of the load.
Flip a three-pickup guitar to an 'in-between' switch setting and two coils combine to cancel hum and produce a hollow, quacky tone neither pickup makes alone.
Orchestra seating, the ground-floor seats nearest the stage, takes its name from the circular ground-level space where chorus stood in ancient Greek theatre.
A curved ceiling or wall can act as an acoustic mirror, concentrating reflected sound into a hot spot in one part of a room while another goes strangely dead.
Robert Moog's ladder filter stacks four matched stages like rungs, and cranking its feedback high enough makes the whole thing self-oscillate into its own tone.
Sound squeezes air so fast that heat has no time to escape between compressions - why the speed of sound follows adiabatic, not isothermal, gas physics.
Demagnetizing tape heads has a ritual: pull the buzzing degausser slowly away before switching it off, or the sudden field can magnetize the heads instead.
Push a speaker into a room corner and bass jumps roughly 6 dB per nearby surface - wall, floor, and a corner can stack toward +18 dB, enough to wreck a mix.
After the last song, a record's groove doesn't just stop - a silent spiral carries the needle inward, often into a locked loop that triggers auto-lift.
An alphorn can only play its natural harmonics, and the 11th one lands stubbornly between F and F-sharp - a note stuck out of tune by nature itself.
A pentode's fifth electrode, the suppressor grid, cured a problem called secondary emission - the fix behind classic tubes like the EL34 and EL84.
Sound waves rippling through the infant universe froze into a cosmic ruler 150 megaparsecs long - astronomers still use that ancient echo to measure space.
Every strip of magnetic tape rides on a plastic backbone whose material tells its age: paper, then acetate, then PVC, then tough polyester by the late '50s.
A hollow instrument's low boost comes from the air trapped inside it resonating like a note blown across a bottle top - the same trick, just built in.
A radio 'cart wall' of instant-play buttons is named for the tape cartridge machines it replaced - the screen still carries the ghost of old hardware.
As a bat or toothed whale closes on prey, its echolocation clicks speed up into a buzz - pulses packed tighter for rapid-fire updates on a moving target.
Two nearby radio signals mixing can leave a steady ghost tone behind - on old recordings it shows up as a whistle near 9-10 kHz from adjacent AM stations.
GPS satellites run on a time scale that never adjusts for leap seconds, so it now sits a fixed 18 seconds ahead of the UTC clock everyone else uses.
Aging lacquer discs can sweat: a greasy white bloom of palmitic acid rising to the surface as the coating's oil breaks down, warning of decay.
Compressed-gas leaks hiss in ultrasound, far above human hearing - point a directional ultrasonic sensor around a pipe and it leads you straight to the leak.
Before it was a software effect, DJ chopping meant slamming a hardware transform switch to cut a sound fully on and off in rapid rhythmic bursts.
Mains hum fluctuates with the power grid's own frequency - checking that pattern, ENF analysis, is one way examiners judge if a recording is genuine.
'Rip and read' comes from literally tearing wire-service copy off a teletype printer and reading it on air almost exactly as it landed, errors and all.
When a collapsing bubble sits near a surface it can't implode evenly - one side punches through, firing a liquid jet at hundreds of meters per second.
Tape recording levels are measured in nanowebers per meter, a magnetic unit so small it takes a billion of them to add up to just one weber.
The early universe was a hot plasma that rang like a bell: gravity squeezed it, light pushed back, and the tug of war set off pressure waves - sound, in effect.
Modular digital multitrack recorders of the 1990s could link together to grow track count - Alesis ADAT on S-VHS tape battled Tascam DTRS on Hi8 for dominance.
Packing a speaker's internal duct with fluffy fibre fill does more than soak up noise - it slows the speed of sound moving through it, lowering the tuning.
Old lacquer records crack in lines radiating from the center as their coating shrinks with age while the rigid disc underneath refuses to shrink with it.
Reshape a supersonic jet's whole airframe and its shock waves stop piling into one sharp crack - the boom lands instead as a stretched, softer thump.
Nixie tubes glow their numerals from stacked, shaped wires in a gas-filled bulb - the name literally short for Numeric Indicator eXperimental No. 1.
Some volcanic tremor isn't noise at all - it settles into a clear musical tone with evenly spaced overtones that glide as the conduit below shifts.
Walter Murch's trick: play clean dialogue out of a speaker into a real room and re-record it there, so a studio voice picks up an actual space's echo.
HVAC hum gets graded like a report card: the Room Criterion number for loudness comes with a letter - N neutral, R rumbly, H hissy, RV rattly.
Tape curling: old tape can warp across its width into a taco shape as the backing and coating age and shrink at different rates.
Rock-art acoustics tests a striking idea: ancient painters favored cave and cliff spots with the strongest echoes, a link that's real but still debated.
Radio 'carts' began as physical endless-loop tape cartridges for instant jingles and IDs - the name outlived the tape, now meaning a software clip.
Some products claim they can hear lying in a person's voice from tiny pitch wobbles - but independent testing has never shown it beats a coin flip.
Philips and Sony's CD-i packed audio, video, text and interactive programs onto a CD for a dedicated TV player - an early-90s format that quietly died.
A sound wave heats the air where it compresses and cools where it stretches - heat quietly leaking between those spots drains energy from the wave itself.
Grid leak bias lets a tube set its own bias automatically through a trickle of grid current, giving old and guitar circuits their touch-sensitive feel.
A sound catchment is a 'viewshed' for the ears - the whole area a place is acoustically linked to, everywhere a listener there could hear or be heard.
A warped wax cylinder can slump out of round into an oval - the stylus rides up and down over the bulge each turn, warbling pitch and risking a skip.
A territorial song does double duty - the same repeated call that warns off rivals and announces the space is taken often attracts a mate at the very same time.
Old crystal mics generated their own voltage from a flexing Rochelle-salt crystal, needing no power at all - fragile, but a strong, self-powered signal.
Blast water with ultrasound and the imploding bubbles get hot enough to rip the molecules apart, forming hydrogen gas and peroxide out of nothing but sound.
Cue wind lets an engineer hear tape at high speed, sped-up and squeaky, so they can spot a word or beat and stop right on it - scrubbing, decades before video.
A band of sharply colder water bends sonar rays downward as they cross it, carving out shadow zones where a submarine can hide from being pinged.
Karplus-Strong fakes a plucked string cheaply: fill a short loop with noise, keep smoothing and repeating it, and it rings and fades like a real pluck.
MRI scanners aren't quiet - their gradient coils slam against the mounts as current switches, often exceeding 100 dB, loud enough to demand earplugs.
Altec Lansing's Mantaray, an early constant-directivity horn from the mid-1970s, was named for a shape that keeps its coverage even across the whole band.
A mic array smaller than its wavelength can still be made surprisingly directional with clever weighting - at the cost of amplifying its own internal noise.
A promo used to mean a real vinyl record stamped for promotional use, given to DJs before release - now it's usually an early file from a digital record pool.
This gas detector listens instead of looking: light gets absorbed, makes a tiny sound, and a microscopic tuning fork rings sharply in reply.
A listening walk is moving through a place in near silence, attending only to its sounds - a method from the acoustic-ecology movement.
Flash a light in perfect step with a vibrating part and it looks frozen solid - stroboscopic imaging lets engineers watch a speaker cone in slow motion.
Bowed-in reel flanges, or just holding a reel by its sides instead of its hub, can pinch the tape pack's edges tight enough to curl and cup them.
An overblow forces a harmonica's normally silent draw reed to sound on an exhale instead, using precise breath control to summon notes it shouldn't have.
The brown magnetic layer on classic tape is essentially rust - tiny iron-oxide particles glued onto a plastic ribbon, magnetized to store sound.
A single pluck on the pipa fades fast, so players fake sustain with lunzhi: rolling all four right-hand fingers across the string to keep one note going.
This test plays two close, high tones and listens for the phantom low tone gear invents - named for a 1930s telephone body later folded into the ITU.
A pistonphone calibrates microphones with one incredibly precise tone, about 124 dB at 250 Hz - and even it needs correcting for the day's air pressure.
Before clean digital sweeps, engineers measured rooms and speakers with MLS - a pseudorandom blast of on/off pulses whose math works even amid background noise.
Pulse light into a sealed gas cell and it heats and cools in step, pressure rising and falling in time - a microphone can literally listen for absorbed light.
Acetate discs, the early instant records, aren't made of acetate at all - they're nitrocellulose lacquer over metal, and the misleading name just stuck.
Helioseismic holography images the Sun's interior by running its surface sound waves backward through a computer - it can even see the far side.
Eisenstein borrowed a music term for film: audiovisual counterpoint, where sound and picture run independent lines of meaning instead of echoing.
Boreholes carry their own named waves, like the Stoneley wave - logging the whole sound wave instead of just its first arrival reveals cracks deep underground.
CD Video packed a few minutes of analog LaserDisc-style video plus digital CD audio onto a gold 12 cm disc - a 1980s hybrid that barely lasted the decade.
Named for its shape, not its sound: a cymbal transducer sandwiches a ceramic disk between two dome-shaped metal caps that turn tiny motion into a big push.
A disc-cutting lathe needs to know the loud parts are coming - a preview head reads the tape one whole turn ahead so it can space grooves wider in time.
Investigators can find a shooter from audio alone, timing the gap between a gunshot's direct blast and its echoes to triangulate the source.
A dummy load is a speaker's silent stunt double: a big resistor that lets an amp get driven hard on the bench, turning the power into heat instead of sound.
Your voice isn't a fingerprint: forensic speaker recognition experts report a match as a likelihood ratio, a strength of evidence, never a certainty.
A theatre's gallery is the narrow catwalk crew use to work the fly ropes and add counterweights - the same word also names the cheap seats up top.
Every bubble underwater rings at its own pitch, like a tiny bell - big bubbles ring low, small ones ring high, which is why rain and waves sound as they do.
Developed at Decca Records in the 1950s, the Decca Tree still anchors film-score recording today - three spaced omni mics in an inverted T, once Neumann M50s.
Some rocks ring like bells when struck - lithophones range from tuned stone bars to natural boulders people played as instruments for millennia.
Old acetate tape can quite literally go sour: as its plastic base breaks down it gives off vinegar syndrome's telltale smell while turning brittle and warped.
A bullet's flight path can be read from sound alone: examiners time its shockwave's arrival angle at several microphones to find the exact line of fire.
Before computers, acousticians built tiny scale models of concert halls and tested them with ultrasonic pitches - shrink the room, raise the frequency to match.
Dialogue editors sync new lines to old footage using one instant: the frame where lips slam fully shut on a p, b, or m - the clearest visual beat a mouth makes.
Old tape backing can crumble with age, shedding fine black dust that clogs heads and guides and can even smear onto the next wrap on the reel.
Every room stamps recordings with its own reverberant fingerprint, so a sudden change in that print, mid-recording, can betray a hidden edit.
R-DAT records digital audio like a VCR records video - a spinning head scans the tape helically, letting small 1980s cassettes hold clean digital sound.
Single-bubble sonoluminescence: trap one bubble in sound and it flashes light every cycle, a picosecond pulse timed to its own violent collapse.
Before the tuba, brass players buzzed into a leather-covered wooden serpent or its keyed successor the ophicleide - both prized for a coarse, rasping growl.
Unlike a trumpet, a woodwind's sound barely comes out its bell at all - most of it leaks out sideways through the open tone holes running down the body.
In a well-wound tape reel every loop lies flush - a popped strand is the one that has slipped sideways and pokes out, ready to get crushed at the next handling.
The qanbus is a short-necked, fretless plucked lute from Yemen, also called the gambus - a centuries-old fixture of Yemeni and wider Arabian music.
A tape machine's rubber pinch roller can wear lopsided - its uneven grip speeds the tape up and slows it down in a steady repeating wobble.
YIG is short for yttrium iron garnet, a magnetic crystal used in microwave gear because a simple applied magnet can smoothly tune its resonance.
The rayl, the unit for how strongly a medium resists sound flow, is one of the few audio units named for a person - the physicist Lord Rayleigh.
A trombone's slide shoots forward on every note, so its mic has to sit safely off to the side - close enough for the bell, but out of the slide's full reach.
Cut a closed circle into the end of a record's spiral and the needle just goes around forever: a locked groove, repeating a segment or silence until lifted.
Shine a laser pulse into tissue and it makes a sound: the sudden heat expansion launches an ultrasound wave that a computer turns into an image.
Around 1925, recording stopped being purely mechanical: a microphone and amplifier fed the cutting head instead of a horn, freeing mic placement from the lathe.
A leaky wave rides along a surface but can't keep its energy to itself - it continuously radiates sound into whatever medium sits against it, fading as it goes.
Laser-scan a ruined historic building, give each surface real acoustic properties, and you can actually listen to how the space sounded before it changed.
Right after an ultrasonic probe fires, it's still ringing and briefly deaf - that dead zone can hide flaws lurking just beneath the surface.
Welsh singer Margaret Watts Hughes built a device to see her own voice: singing into its stretched membrane made powder form patterns like flowers and ferns.
A tube open at one end and sealed at the other only rings at odd harmonics - the mismatched pressure at each end is what shapes the resonance.
Lab-grade measurement mic capsules are commonly charged at 200 volts DC - far beyond the 48V phantom power that runs an ordinary studio condenser.
A ringstone is a boulder that rings like a bell when struck - dense, crack-free rock vibrating so cleanly that people once played it as an instrument.
Before automated consoles, 'recall' meant an assistant photographing every knob on an analog desk so the whole mix could be rebuilt by hand next session.
A septuplet delay locks its echoes to seven equal steps per beat or bar, an odd, rolling subdivision that deliberately fights against the main groove.
A 'loop unit' in ADR still carries the ghost of film's physical loops - actors once rehearsed against an actual short length of looped film.
A phased-array probe steers and focuses its beam purely electronically, firing hundreds of tiny elements in precise sequence, without ever physically moving.
Play a tape recorded on a differently aligned machine and its treble fades - some transfer systems now servo the head or fix it in software instead.
Sound waves rippling through the infant universe froze in place at a fixed radius as it cooled, leaving galaxies clustered at that same distance ever since.
Alnico speaker magnets - aluminum, nickel and cobalt - give up a little magnetism under hard use, and that gentle compression is the vintage sound people chase.
The anvil is a tiny bone in your middle ear, sitting between the hammer and the stirrup, quietly relaying every sound vibration toward your inner ear.
Gunther Theile's OCT array turns its side mics outward, away from each other, on purpose - starving the left and right channels of crosstalk before it starts.
Astronomers measure a star's insides in time, not distance - acoustic radius is simply how long sound takes to travel from the core out to a given layer.
The Gray Audograph: a 1940s office-dictation disc recorded at a variable speed on its own proprietary machine, useless anywhere else and now nearly unplayable.
Even calm ocean water isn't silent - the random jostling of water molecules themselves adds a faint hiss to the sea's constant background noise.
The tape machine is long gone from most stages, but the operator who once threaded it is still called the tape op, even when running a laptop.
Ultrasound can blend oil and water without stirring - cavitation shreds one liquid into droplets so fine they stay suspended in the other.
A talk box doesn't process sound electronically - it pipes real amplifier sound through a tube into the player's mouth, shaped by lips, then re-miked.
Cymatic response is the whole vocabulary of patterns a plate or puddle draws as you sweep its driving pitch - a physical portrait of sound made visible.
The thin, slippery liner sheets inside a cassette can warp with heat or age - once they stop lying flat, they drag on the tape and the pitch wobbles.
Some concert halls sit on giant springs or rubber pads, floating the entire building to isolate it from subway rumble and street traffic.
A layer impression is a tiny dent pressed permanently into tape by grit or a splice edge sitting in the layer wound right next to it.
Blending a re-recorded studio line into a noisy location scene works like patching a photo - matching level, room tone, and reverb until the seam disappears.
Old dictation belts creased flat in storage can sometimes be coaxed straight with gentle warming - though the wrong plastic or too much heat ruins them.
Acoustemology, fusing 'acoustic' and 'epistemology', is the theory that people come to know a place, a relationship, even themselves, chiefly through listening.
Some big vacuum tubes route their plate connection to a shiny cap right on top of the glass in plain sight - and it can sit at 400 to 800 volts.
A tanpura's drone doesn't just decay, it blooms - strings brushing a curved bridge grow shimmering overtones mid-note, like a chord slowly opening.
Shave the base film thin enough and roughly three times the usual tape fits on one reel - at the cost of a tape far more prone to stretching and curling.
Drummers can fake a double kick pedal with just one foot: rock it heel-down for the first stroke, then let the toes catch the second, both in a single motion.
Tape machines go silent during fast-wind on purpose - a tiny lifter pin pulls the tape off the heads so it doesn't scream past at high speed.
The Katzenklavier, or cat piano, was a hypothetical instrument: press a key and a caged cat, arranged by pitch, would yowl on cue - mercifully never built.
The Voigt pipe: a tapered quarter-wave speaker cabinet from the 1930s, named for its inventor, tuned like a stubby foghorn working in reverse.
Some stage mics are deliberately pointed the 'wrong' way, away from the crowd, aiming their dead rear zone at the PA speakers for extra gain before feedback.
A single-ended amp stage uses one output device for the whole waveform - simple, low power, prized for the warm even-harmonic tone of single-ended-triode amps.
A clarinet's closed cylindrical bore overblows a twelfth; a saxophone's cone-shaped bore overblows a clean octave instead - same trick, different leap.
Wound tightly on a reel, a loud passage can quietly magnetize the layer touching it - so you hear a faint pre-echo of what's coming, seconds early.
Archaeologists sometimes build playable replicas of ancient instruments from fragments and carvings alone, filling evidence gaps with informed guesswork.
"Volt-ohm-milliammeter" is the old full name for what everyone just calls a multimeter today - a name that predates the digital multimeter it now describes.
Mix engineers often work from a glass booth at the back of the house - sealed off for control, but hearing a different room sound than the audience out front.
A vactrol pairs a tiny glowing LED with a light-sensitive resistor sealed in one capsule, so one circuit can control another using nothing but light.
A double attack fires two hits for one strike - convincing enough to be mistaken for a flam, the real drum rudiment where a soft grace note leads the main hit.
That snappy click at the start of a Hammond organ note isn't a flaw - it's contacts chopping a tone that was already sounding, and it's essential to the sound.
A black box has one microphone that just listens to the whole cockpit - alarms, switch clicks, engine roar - separate from each pilot's own mic.
A tape delay's echo time isn't a knob value - it's the physical gap between a record head and a playback head on the same moving loop of tape.
A North African bendir frame drum gets its buzzy sizzle from gut strings stretched under the head, rattling against it like a built-in snare.
Early-1980s digital reverb didn't always fade gently - its tail could hold steady or cut off abruptly instead, a sound instantly tied to that decade.
A standing sound wave has silent points called nodes - small heavy particles drift into them and get held there, motionless, by sound alone.
Hammond organs add a short, bell-like 'ping' at the start of a note called percussion - but it fires once, so holding two keys down silences it.
The loudest part of a fast jet's exhaust isn't the engine - it's Mach waves, beamed sound thrown out when turbulent eddies outrun the speed of sound.
One word, three lives: a five-cent movie theatre, a coin-operated player piano, and - by extension - a jukebox.
Biophony is every sound made by living things in a habitat - birdsong, insect buzz, frog calls - one of three soundscape layers coined by Bernie Krause.
Disc-cutting styluses were sometimes gently warmed by a built-in heater, like warming a knife before slicing, so they'd glide through lacquer with less noise.
The Sun has a pitch ceiling near 5.3 mHz: sound waves below it stay trapped inside, unable to escape, while waves above it leak outward into space.
Old tape copies don't reveal their place in line by sound quality alone - archivists read box notes and leader tape to judge how many dubs back a reel sits.
Some subway tracks sit on a concrete raft that itself rests on springs, so the whole slab bounces slowly and trains never shake the buildings above.
'House to half' is the stage manager's call to dim audience lights to about 50% just before curtain, a quiet nudge telling the crowd to settle in.
Volcanoes, impacts and wind make infrasound on other worlds too - but sound needs a gas to travel, so it can never cross the vacuum between planets.
Long before digital plugins had a 'chamber' reverb setting, studios built small, hard, reflective rooms and piped sound through them for natural echo.
Beam steering aims a microphone array at a target using tiny timed delays between elements, not motors - the array points itself without a single moving part.
Cutting vinyl, an elliptical equalizer folds deep bass toward the groove's center, since out-of-phase bass can throw the cutting or playback stylus off.
Sound travels faster through warm air than cold, so a speaker delay set correctly in the afternoon can drift out of alignment by the time evening cools down.
A microscope maps an old record's groove in 3D, then software runs a virtual stylus through that shape to recover the audio - no needle ever touches it.
Chirp sonar sends a swooping frequency sweep, then squeezes the returning echo into a sharp peak - fine range detail without sacrificing transmitted power.
Old-school techs still hunt a dead amplifier stage by feeding it a buzzy test tone and working backward from the speaker until the tone goes silent.
Sound waves rippling across a patch of the Sun's surface form ring-shaped patterns in a 3D chart - hidden currents below subtly warp those rings.
Upstage means toward the back of the stage - a leftover from centuries when stages were literally built on a slope, so the rear was physically higher.
Some rooms retune themselves on command: a motor unrolls a curtain of absorptive fabric to deaden a room for speech, then retracts it for a livelier sound.
RCA once squeezed four channels of quadraphonic sound onto a single vinyl disc, hiding the rear channels inside an ultrasonic subcarrier.
Sprinkle fine powder on a vibrating plate and it dances into pictures: grains pile up on the still lines, tracing a resonance's shape by eye.
Skeuomorphism is why your phone's camera still fakes a shutter click, a sound with no function left, kept purely to feel familiar from a physical original.
A resonator banjo's rounded back isn't cosmetic - it acts like a bowl, throwing sound forward and making it far louder and punchier than an open-backed one.
On a pipe organ, pulling a knob called a 'stop' lets a whole rank of pipes sound - the literal origin of the phrase 'pulling out all the stops.'
A toothed whale clicks through its nose, not its mouth, then aims the sound with a fatty forehead lens called the melon before listening for the echo.
Old church pulpits sometimes had a canopy overhead called a tester, built to catch a preacher's unamplified voice and project it out to the congregation.
Optoacoustic imaging turns light into sound - a laser pulse makes tissue flash-expand, and the resulting ultrasonic wave is captured to build an image of it.
Every position on a stage is measured from the 'plaster line' - though despite the name, it usually sits at bare proscenium framing, nowhere near real plaster.
A bipole speaker fires matching drivers from two opposite faces in phase, both pushing outward together for a wide, diffuse, nearly omnidirectional spread.
Tape pulled from cold storage must warm up slowly while still sealed in its bag, or it sweats condensation on itself like a cold soda can in summer.
A cave's impulse response is its acoustic fingerprint: fire one short sound, capture the tangle of echoes and decay, and reuse it later as a reverb.
Above every fly-tower stage hides a walkable steel-grate ceiling, the grid deck, where crews stand to service the pulleys the audience never sees.
Some choir sample libraries don't just hold vowels - a syllable-sequencing engine spells out real words, so the virtual choir seems to sing your actual lyrics.
SSL built a brutal compressor into its consoles just to tame the talkback mic - until Hugh Padgham caught a drummer through it and helped define 1980s pop.
Despite the name, Helmholtz instability isn't a resonating bottle - it's rolling vortices where two air streams slide past each other, seeding jet noise.
Set a tape machine's bias too low and you get a strange trade: brighter, boosted highs, paid for with more distortion and a shakier recording.
When only the last few words of a take go wrong, editors don't always redo the whole line - they record just that broken tail and splice it onto the good start.
Some old records can now be played without a needle ever touching them: a flat photograph of the groove's wiggle is enough for software to recover the sound.
Scientists scan the Sun's interior by timing sound waves crossing its surface between two points - listening to structure you'll never actually see.
A voiceprint is really just a picture of a voice's frequencies - once sold as an ID sure as a fingerprint, though scientists warn it isn't nearly that certain.
Clap in front of a flight of steps and the echoes from each riser arrive so fast they blur into a descending chirp - famous at Mayan pyramids.
Old telephone exchanges routed calls with X-Y switches: a wiper moved one way to pick a row, then another way to pick a column, like a mechanical grid.
Frozen ground cracks as it freezes and thaws, and each tiny fracture fires a faint high-pitched burst - sensors count them to catch instability early.
A warped or cheap cassette shell can hold the tape at a slight slant against the playback head - and that tiny tilt alone is enough to quietly fade the treble.
A roaring volcanic mudflow of boulders and water radiates sound too low to hear - sensors track this lahar infrasound down the valley as an early warning.
Two mics face a spinning Leslie cabinet from opposite sides, each hearing the horn swing toward and away, together capturing its swirl in stereo.
Broadcast engineers keep a strict direction sense: a contribution feed flows into the station from the field, lightly compressed since it still has to be mixed.
DASH, Sony's 1980s open-reel digital format, used fixed heads rather than DAT's spinning ones - it powered machines like the PCM-3324 and PCM-3348.
Sound near the deep sound channel's axis, where ocean sound speed bottoms out, stays trapped and can travel thousands of kilometers - how whales call so far.
Most records play outer edge inward, but some radio transcription discs run the opposite way - groove starting near the label and spiraling outward to the rim.
A bucket mute is literally a padded cup clipped over a trumpet's bell, muffling it into a soft, dark, veiled tone - like hanging a blanket in front of the horn.

Rectified diffusion: a sound-driven bubble can slowly grow instead of dissolving, absorbing slightly more gas while ballooning than it releases while shrinking.

OTL tube amps skip the usual bulky output transformer and drive speakers almost directly - which means stacking many tubes just to survive the mismatch.
Cassotto: Italian for 'little house,' a hidden chamber inside a fine accordion that reeds sound through, warming the tone like singing into cupped hands.

Reznikoff and Dauvois found that painted spots in prehistoric caves often sit exactly where the echo is strongest - art placed by ear, maybe.

Harsh, exaggerated 'sss' and 'tss' sounds in the high end - like the sound is literally spitting at you.

Backward masking: a sound played right after a brief tone can still hide it - a later noise can erase something you already heard.

Big stage houses keep a whole second stage hidden right behind the first - a full-size wagon holding an entire preset scene, ready to roll forward on cue.

Old ADR sessions cued actors with an actual punch: a hole flashed into the film at the sync frame, backed by a streamer and three countdown beeps.

Lacquer crackers: old studio slang for phonograph records, straight from the lacquer-coated discs a cutting stylus once engraved them onto.

A concave dome or curved wall bounces sound the way a curved mirror bounces light, concentrating reflections into one spot far louder than the rest.

Sandy, or grainy, describes a sound that feels made of tiny rough particles rather than being smooth - like a photo full of specks instead of a clean picture.

Rain-on-the-roof excitation: engineers model a structure hit by countless small, unrelated random taps everywhere at once - exactly like actual rain on a roof.

A diffuser panel covered in blocks of wildly different heights, like a tiny city skyline, that scatters sound in every direction instead of absorbing it.

Cardboard tone: engineer slang for a drum so dead and boxy it sounds like someone struck an actual cardboard box instead of a real drum.
Chordophone: the classification for ancient string instruments like lyres and harps - identified mostly from wear marks, since the strings rot away.

Misdirection audio steers guests' ears toward one spot in a haunted attraction so a scare can spring from the direction they aren't looking.
Translationese is the tell-tale sound of a bad dub: dialogue that's accurate but stiff, over-explained, full of odd phrasing that gives away it was translated.

The first physical copy of a mastered record isn't vinyl - it's an aluminum disc coated in soft lacquer, later electroplated into the metal press parts.

Thumpy names a sound itself: a low-end thump so strong you feel the kick or bass, praised as punch when it's tight and mocked as boom when it isn't.
Polish TV still favours lektor: one flat narrator reads every character's lines over the original soundtrack, still faintly audible underneath.
Before plastic, magnetic tape was recorded onto strips of paper - a fragile 1930s and 40s format that can tear if handled like modern tape.
The Jit is a footwork dance from Detroit, built on rapid, intricate steps and kicks to up-tempo music - born alongside the city's own dance-music scene.
Resonator guitars built around one metal cone come in two flavors: 'biscuit,' with the bridge on the cone's tip, or 'spider,' a bridge splayed across its rim.
Chesty names a voice with too much low-midrange weight - it sounds heavy, congested, like the sound is rumbling straight up out of someone's chest.

Dubbing teams must decide what to do with honorifics like Japanese -san: keep them, drop them, or swap in a different mark of respect.

Two microphones set a little apart hear the same sound at very slightly different instants - that tiny time gap alone is enough to calculate its direction.
A tab, or tableau, curtain doesn't part flat or fly straight up - diagonal lines pull it up and out into draped, festooned swags at the corners.

Harmonic bloom describes a note's overtones opening up as it sustains or gets driven harder - like a flower unfurling, richer the longer it rings.

Gavrilov translation is a 1980s-90s Russian video convention: one flat-voiced narrator reads every character's lines over the still-audible original soundtrack.

Theatre wings are numbered from downstage back, so the confusingly-named third wing is actually the third hidden entrance far upstage, not near the front.
A Hardanger fiddle hides extra strings beneath the fingerboard that are never bowed - they just ring in sympathy, giving the instrument its shimmering glow.
Gong-y: engineer-speak for a sound that swells and shimmers like a struck gong, its metallic overtones ringing on in a long, spreading wash.
Some foreign films are dubbed not from the original language but from an English 'pivot' version - a translation of a translation.
Flow phonation is the vocal sweet spot between breathy and pressed - the folds close just enough to vibrate freely, giving a strong sound with no strain.

One diode, three nicknames - freewheeling, catch, or snubber - all for the same part that gives a switched-off coil's stored current somewhere safe to go.

Foldback is the British term for stage monitoring - the mix sent back toward performers so they can hear themselves and each other over the crowd.

Your ear isn't one microphone, it's hundreds: the cochlea behaves like a bank of overlapping filters, each tuned to its own narrow slice of pitch.
A grain cloud is a swarm of tiny sound particles heard as one shifting texture - like a cloud of gnats that reads as a single shape from a distance.

Incomplete erasure leaves a faint ghost of whatever was on a tape before, haunting supposedly blank tape beneath the new recording.

A battle mix isn't for the dancefloor - it's a DJ showing off scratching, beat juggling and razor-sharp cuts purely to outdo a rival in competition.

A spring reverb makes its echo by physically shaking sound down a metal spring, like the twang of a screen door, turning motion back into music.
Loudspeakers put sound out in the room without trying; headphones often fail to, leaving voices stuck inside your head unless the right spatial cues are added.
A "dead wedge" is live-sound slang for the angled floor monitor that's gone silent on a performer - the culprit is usually a muted aux send, not a blown driver.
A bridle hangs a load from two rigging legs instead of one - widen the angle past 90 degrees and each leg's tension climbs fast, nearly doubling near 150.
HIFU focuses ultrasound to a single point inside the body precisely enough to heat and destroy tissue there - surgery done with sound, no incision needed.
Some old cylinder records hide a plaster core under a thin celluloid shell - if it absorbs damp air and swells, the shell can crack from the inside out.
Jump a parameter instantly and you get 'zipper noise' - a stepped, crackling artifact named for its sound. Smoothing ramps the change gently instead.
Shrinking a file to fewer bits creates crackly distortion in quiet passages; dither trades that away by adding a tiny hiss the ear simply tunes out as noise.
Sonofragmentation: ultrasound alone can shatter pharmaceutical crystals into smaller particles, the shockwaves from collapsing bubbles doing the smashing.
Every bowed note carries scratch and hiss from rosin and hair dragging the string - engineers place the mic to keep just enough of that grit, not to erase it.
Digging in the crates is the hip-hop ritual of flipping through boxes of obscure vinyl, hunting for the one drum break or sample worth building a track around.
Dubbing has to land p, b and m sounds exactly where the actor's lips visibly close - the tightest constraint in matching a new voice to a face on screen.
The classic 1957 EMT plate reverb makes echo by shaking an entire suspended steel sheet and listening to it ring with contact pickups.
Studio slang for a dull, boxy, lifeless tone - one that sounds uncannily like knocking on the side of an empty cardboard box.
Not every harmonic matters equally for pitch - a middle band near 500 Hz to 2 kHz dominates, so pitch tracks it even when other partials drift.
Take the spectrum of a spectrum and you get a cepstrum, measured not in frequency but in 'quefrency' - a scrambled word for a deliberately inverted idea.
A reverse-log, or anti-log, pot is a volume knob wired backwards - most of its change happens at the start of the turn, not the end.
In a music room, jamming means improvising freely with other players - on a radio engineer's channel it means someone is deliberately blocking the signal.
A phonon is one quantum packet of vibration in a crystal - sound and heat in a solid actually travel as swarms of these countable little units.
Feed both ears a fast train of clicks and your brain barely uses most of them - it leans on the first few to judge direction, tuning out the rest.
A "flip" is dance-music slang for reworking someone else's track or acappella into a new edit, bootleg, or remix with a fresh arrangement or genre.
Acoustic shock disorder can follow one sudden loud sound in a headset - call-centre workers first reported it - yet the ear often tests normal afterward.
Minnaert resonance: a bubble in water rings like a tiny bell, trapped gas acting as the spring - it's the physics behind the babble of a brook.
Microsound names a scale of sound most people never think about - shorter than what you'd call a note, but longer than a single digital sample.
Old acetate discs slowly poison themselves: as the oil that keeps their lacquer soft evaporates, it shrinks, cracks, and sheds a greasy white bloom.
A reverb's 'bloom' is how its density builds gradually after the sound hits, swelling fuller a moment later instead of arriving all at once.
Push noise reduction too hard and it leaves little warbling tones behind called birdies - a fake chirp traded for the hiss it was meant to remove.
Invented in the 1850s, the phonautograph was the first machine to record sound - it drew the waves as a line on a cylinder but could never play them back.
A shadow zone is a patch of ocean sound simply cannot bend into - refraction steers every ray around it, so a target hiding there is nearly undetectable.
Some digital compression can make a sound leak backward in time - a faint smear of noise appears just before a sharp drum hit, called pre-echo.
Before software, dubbing actors read from a literal ribbon of 35mm film text scrolling past a cue line - a French technique now done on screen.
Two speaker drivers with a sealed pocket of trapped air between them, moving in lockstep - the isobaric trick halves the box size for a given sound.
A drum or cymbal hit that smears out of focus instead of snapping clean - the sound of an attack pushed so hard it splatters.
Before actors record a dubbed line, someone reads the script aloud just to catch tongue-twisters and lines too long to say in a single breath.
Voiceprint analysis compares speech spectrograms to identify a speaker - but experts warn that matching them by eye alone isn't reliable proof in court.
Switching hash is the harsh gritty buzz that light dimmers and cheap power supplies leak into audio as they chop mains power on and off fast.
Synchresis, coined by Michel Chion, names how a sound and image landing at the same instant feel bonded together, even when nothing really connects them.
Some loudspeaker arrays can aim sound at one exact seat, loud and clear, while a neighboring seat gets almost none of it - no headphones required.
When a cassette's plastic shell cracks or seizes, archivists give it a shell transplant - moving the tape and hubs into a fresh, working case.
Xylophone and marimba makers undercut each bar's underside to bend its overtones into musical ratios - a twelfth for xylophone, two octaves for marimba.
Stiction is the extra grip that must be broken before two surfaces start sliding - it's why old, sticky tape can cling stubbornly to the playback heads.
Half-dubbing translates only what's essential, sliding the new line into the original soundtrack's silent gaps instead of replacing the dialogue outright.
A reverb's 'Spin' knob doesn't spin anything you can see - it just wanders the internal delay taps around, so long tails never lock into a metallic ring.
Your inner ear generates its own tiny electrical signal that mirrors the incoming sound wave almost exactly - as if the cochlea were literally a microphone.
That shiny silver patch inside a vacuum tube is the getter, a chemical flashed to soak up leftover gas - turned chalky white, the tube is dead.
A collapsing cavitation bubble crushes its trapped gas so fast that heat can't escape, flashing its tiny core to extreme temperature and pressure in an instant.
Push a voice hard enough and it stops sounding smooth - it breaks into a string of tiny audible beads, fittingly called vocal granulation.
Hi-lo sirens don't sweep, they snap between two fixed pitches about once a second, a two-tone pattern common on European emergency vehicles.
There's a name for weaponizing sound against people: sonic control spans calming background music to piercing anti-loitering devices built to drive you away.
Oskar Heil's air-motion transformer speaker squeezes air from a pleated diaphragm's folds, ejecting it several times faster than the diaphragm itself moves.
A hair microphone is exactly that - a tiny mic tucked into an actor's hairline so it vanishes from camera while still catching every word clearly.
DSL means Downstage Left: front of stage, performer's left. Stage directions follow the performer facing out, so stage left is actually the audience's right.
Opposing ocean swells collide far out at sea and generate a steady infrasound hum near 0.2 Hz, a background heartbeat infrasound arrays hear worldwide.
Some magnetic materials change size when magnetized, and change magnetism when squeezed - early sonar used this two-way effect to make sound underwater.
Room-tone pumping is background ambience that rises and falls under dialogue, as if the room itself were breathing - a sign of over-hard noise reduction.
Let the smoke out: shop slang for frying a component, riffing on the joke that electronics run on magic smoke - once it escapes, the part is dead.
Make one ear hear a sound sooner, or the other ear louder, and you can drag its perceived location back toward center - timing and loudness cues trade off.
Some sounds have no pitch or instrument name to describe them - spectromorphology gives composers words for how a sound's shape rises, moves, and dies away.
Taboo calibration decides how strong a curse lands in a dub - some markets keep it raw, some soften it to a euphemism, some cut it, all by local custom.
Some ancient routes were built to change how they sound as you walk - a tight passage suddenly opening into a booming chamber, on purpose.
Sniff the line: troubleshooting slang for probing a signal chain point by point with an audio probe until you find exactly where the sound goes missing.
Skilled players nudge notes sharp or flat on purpose, pulling a leading tone up or a chord pure, so real performances depart measurably from equal temperament.
Vinyl lathes get a head start: a second playback head reads the program one revolution ahead, warning the cutter to widen the groove before loud parts.
'Ice cream' and 'I scream' can sound nearly identical spoken aloud - an oronym, proof that speech has no real gaps between its words.
Paila literally means "metal pan" in Spanish - it's the Cuban name for timbales, and by extension the metal shell players tap for the clicky cascara pattern.
A narthex is the entrance hall of a church, between the outer doors and the nave - historically a holding space for those not yet admitted to the congregation.
Crowd extras mumble nonsense like 'rhubarb rhubarb' or 'peas and carrots' to fill a scene with background chatter that has no real, distracting words.
A center cluster hangs every PA speaker together above the stage, so the sound is perceived as coming from the performer beneath it, not from off to the sides.
Touring engineers joke about the 'desk du jour' - whatever mixing console a venue happens to hand them that day, learned cold with zero rehearsal time.
Cavitation almost always needs a seed - a speck of trapped gas in dust or a scratch. A truly pure, gas-free liquid resists forming a bubble at all.
Old microphone spec sheets rated sensitivity in decibels per microbar - a pressure unit equal to one-millionth of a bar, now all but forgotten in acoustics.
Boost certain frequency bands and a sound seems to jump above or behind you, whatever its true position - Blauert mapped these direction-biasing bands by ear.
A thermophone makes sound with no moving diaphragm at all - a current heats and cools a thin wire so fast that the air itself pulses into sound.
Lip sync has a formal dubbing name: phonetic synchronization, just one of three classic 'synchronies' alongside isochrony and kinesic synchrony.
A shake is a lead trumpet trick: rapidly wobbling between a note and the one above by shaking lips or horn, usually thrown in at the top of a loud phrase.
"Glassy" means bright, clear treble with a hard, shiny edge - smooth yet strangely brittle at once, like the sound has the actual texture of glass.
A collapsing cavitation bubble briefly reaches several thousand kelvin and cools by over a billion degrees a second - gone again in under a microsecond.
Squeezing a translated line to fit an actor's mouth and timing can quietly kill the joke or wordplay - dubbers call this adaptation loss.
Early sonographs had no screen at all: they swept a filter across the spectrum and literally burned the frequency picture onto paper as it played.
A chromagram throws away which octave a note sits in and shows only its letter name - a computer's way of hearing chord and key the way our ears group pitch.
Notes and attacks that blur together instead of landing clean and separate - all the crunch has gone soggy.
Out-of-phase bass can shake a stylus out of its groove, so vinyl mastering sums deep bass to mono - the low end cuts louder without derailing the needle.
Archaeologists now pair what a site could be seen from with what it could be heard from - mapping a soundshed right alongside the visual viewshed.
Ohmage: old British slang for a loudspeaker's resistance rating, long since retired in favor of the more accurate word impedance.
The rebab, a small bowed spike fiddle, makes a thin, nasal tone engineers just call a whine - born from a tiny body and harmonic-rich bowed strings.
A room full of echoes still lets you point straight at a voice, because your ear trusts only the first arrival for direction and quietly fuses the rest into it.
Beatmatched records drift apart the moment you let go, so a DJ nudges the tempo control by ear to hold the lock - a skill the sync button nearly retired.
Engineers call it bloom: the way a hall's reverb keeps swelling after a loud note before settling into decay - too much and it swallows the next entrance.
Dubbed sync doesn't need to be frame-perfect - close-ups allow almost no drift, but an off-screen or wide-shot line can wander and still read as natural.
Humpback song stacks small units into phrases and phrases into themes, like sentences - and those themes keep changing and spreading between groups over time.
Reach for a stock scream from a sound library and you might unknowingly grab the Wilhelm scream - recognizable enough to distract an audience outright.
Live theatre speakers deliberately play an actor's voice a beat late - the Haas effect then makes the amplified sound seem to come from the actor, not the PA.
To "ohm-out" a cable is slang for testing it end to end on a meter's resistance setting - confirming conductors are continuous and nothing shorts.
Speed up a track with key lock off and it slides upward like a chipmunk - the feature time-stretches the audio so tempo can change without the pitch following.
Researchers rebuild the entire soundscape of a vanished place - not one room but a whole environment - modeling how every sound once carried across it.
Before automatic mic mixers, theatre engineers followed the script by hand, opening only the speaking actor's microphone and muting it again after.
A PFX pull is a dialogue editor's hunt through on-set audio for usable footsteps, door clunks, and prop handling, salvaged onto their own effects track.
The brown note is a supposed infrasonic tone said to make anyone hearing it lose bowel control - a beloved urban legend no study has ever confirmed.
Old synths speak in control voltage, one volt per octave; a CV-to-MIDI box reads it and outputs MIDI notes, letting analog gear drive digital rigs.
An accordion's air button releases the bellows silently, except for the soft hiss of escaping air a close mic can pick up as a whisper between notes.
Bats sweep pitch up or down within a single call - the changing frequency itself sharpens their sense of a target's exact range and shape.
Film composers write phrases with stretchy internal timing, so a stretch can lengthen or shorten a cue to hit a new picture edit without a rewrite.
Frisson is the shiver or goosebumps a great musical moment can trigger - a measurable physical response researchers use as evidence music is moving someone.
The Jecklin disk parks a solid baffle between two mics to shadow sound the way your own head shadows it between your ears, building stereo from that shadow.
A sneak step is a Foley footstep performed on purpose too quietly - soft, careful, toe-to-heel contact that tells the audience a character is hiding.
The f-shaped holes on a violin or archtop guitar aren't just decoration - much of the low end escapes through them, acting like the ported vents on a speaker.
Sonorous describes a sound that's full, deep and rich, heavy with sustained low and midrange body - a judgment call, not a measurement.
Dubbing has to redo more than words - honorifics and formal versus casual speech get rebuilt so the new language keeps the same social distance.
Crew slang for a fault or fix nobody can explain - it comes and goes for no known reason, and calling it voodoo admits it will probably come back.
Sound can wander into a dead-end space in the head, like blocked nostrils, and never get out - the trapped energy leaves a voice sounding muffled or tinny.
MIDI chase has a sequencer starting mid-song rewind through earlier patch and pedal changes, so the instrument wakes in the right state, not the wrong one.
Strike a darbuka near the center and you get a doum - a deep boom named for the sound itself, the low twin of the sharp, rim-struck tek.
A pickup sitting where a string harmonic barely moves picks up almost none of it - the real physics behind why bridge pickups sound bright, neck ones warm.
A Live-End-Dead-End control room deadens the front near the speakers to kill early reflections while the rear stays lively and diffusive - a literal dead end.
The vertical channel fader on a DJ mixer is called an upfader - a name borrowed straight from stage-lighting terminology, not DJ culture at all.
Deep inside a very reverberant room, sound arrives from every direction at once with equal strength - no clear spot you could point to and call the source.
A trick mix turns the seam between two songs into the moment itself: scratches, spinbacks and rewinds performed on purpose instead of hidden.
Rhonchisonant is an archaic word meaning 'sounding like a snort or a snore' - a rare bit of vocabulary for describing a rough, growly sonic character.
Tin Pan Alley got its name from the tinny clatter of cheap pianos in the New York publishing district that shaped American pop song for decades.
Some dialogue is baked permanently into a film's music-and-effects track, like text printed into a photo - dubbers can't peel it back out.
A boxy, nasal tone with heavy midrange and thin lows and highs - the signature sound of a small phone speaker.
Every chorus, flanger, and Leslie effect secretly relies on the Doppler effect - stretching a delay's length over time bends pitch, like a passing siren.
Yelp is a real siren setting - the same pitch sweep as a wail, just cycled many times faster, which is why it reads as more urgent in traffic.
Pauline Oliveros drew a sharp line between hearing, which just happens, and listening, an active skill trained through meditation and improvisation.
A goniometer draws your stereo signal as a moving shape on screen - a tall narrow trace means mono-safe, a flat horizontal one means the channels are fighting.
A ship's general emergency alarm is oddly specific: seven short blasts and one long one, sounded on horns and bells until every soul reaches a muster station.
A 'wild' pickup is dialogue deliberately recorded out of sync, just to grab a missed or better line, then quietly dropped into the scene during editing.
In a strange minority of listeners, two ears hear worse than one - a paradox called binaural interference, where the brain garbles what should help.
Countless sound paths leave a source, but only a few actually reach the listener - those true connectors are eigenrays, each with its own delay and strength.
B plus is the high-voltage supply feeding a tube's plate - and it can stay lethally charged in the filter capacitors long after the amp is unplugged.
Deep in the ocean sits a layer of minimum sound speed that bends sound back toward it, letting a call cross thousands of kilometers almost undiminished.
The ganza shuffle drives Brazilian samba by shaking a tube rattle forward and back so both strokes sound, laying down a nonstop rustle under the beat.
Shake a harmonica fast between two neighboring holes and the two notes blur into a shimmering trill players call a warble, or a shake.
Ohm's acoustic law: scramble the phase of a steady tone's harmonics and your ear barely notices, yet the same scrambling turns obvious on sharp transients.
Spectral healing works like Photoshop's healing brush for audio: paint over a damaged patch in a spectrogram and software rebuilds it from the sound around it.
Tip a rainstick slowly and its beads cascade past internal thorns, producing a soft rushing hiss engineered to mimic the sound of actual falling rain.
Game engines carve spaces into 'rooms' with their own reverb, linked by 'portals' - doorways that decide how much sound and echo leak between them.
Remove an actor's voice track to dub it and you also lose their footsteps and prop sounds - so Foley artists rebuild every one of them by hand from scratch.
A master lacquer is so soft it can barely be played at all - the fragile groove that seeds every pressed record gets copied onto tougher metal instead.
Your voice starts as rapid puffs of air chopped by vibrating vocal folds - the glottal source - which your mouth then filters into vowels and words.
Early on you can hear each echo off a wall on its own - mixing time is roughly the moment they pile up too thick to tell apart and blur into a single wash.
Isochrony: a dubbed line must match the original's timing exactly, pauses included - like pouring new words into a cup that can't overflow.
Sprinkle grains on a shaking plate and they don't just jitter in place - they slowly crawl toward the calm spots, pulled by forces only visible over time.
Play only the overtones of a bass note and leave the fundamental out entirely - your brain still hears the low pitch that was never actually there.
Named for a tube whose gain, its mu, drops as its grid is biased more negative - the signal's own level quietly turns the tube's amplification down.
A calque doesn't just borrow a phrase from another language - a structural one imports its grammar too, and the copied pattern can end up sounding normal.
Like a police lineup, but for voices: a witness hears the suspect hidden among several similar-sounding foils and says whether they recognize it.
That slash mark ( / ) sitting quietly inside S/PDIF and A/D has an actual name most people never learn: the solidus.
Decaying acetate tape and film literally start to smell like vinegar as it breaks down - and the acid released speeds decay in tapes stored nearby.
Good dubbing translates silence too - scripts mark exactly how long a character stays quiet on screen, so new words never spill into a pause that wasn't there.
Sound with its clear top end missing, as if a thin curtain were hung between you and the music - dull, distant, faintly muffled.
Talk fast and casual and your tongue never quite arrives - vowel sounds fall short of their target and blur toward neutral, a slip called formant undershoot.
"Pinning it" is road-crew slang for pushing a signal so hard the level meter slams flat against its top stop - a visual siren for overload and clipping.
Orotund is the word for a voice that fills the room - full, round, resonant, the sound of a classic radio announcer.
The sarangi's dozens of sympathetic strings ring on their own beneath the bowed melody, wrapping each note in a soft, cloudy wash of unbidden overtones.
Shamisen players strike the string and body together with a huge pick, the bachi, adding a sharp, drum-like slap to the front of every note.
Early wax cylinders are so fragile some are too risky to touch with a stylus at all - their audio is instead recovered by scanning with light.
Sample a tone above the Nyquist limit and it doesn't vanish - it folds back down as a spurious, unrelated pitch, mirrored around that point.
A yoke isn't just the U-bracket that aims a hung speaker - the same word names the coil around a CRT's neck and the windings around a transformer's core.
A warble tone wobbles its pitch back and forth on purpose - the wandering frequency smears out sharp room resonances so a meter isn't fooled by a null.
To wax a disc means to cut a record - a phrase left over from when the master groove really was carved into a blank of wax, not lacquer.
A spindex plays just the sound of a list item's first letter before speaking the whole thing, so you can zip through a spoken alphabetical menu by ear alone.
When old splicing-tape glue softens in storage, it can weld one loop of tape to the next - unwinding fights the very join meant to hold it together.

term: Not enough rig for the gig
body: 'Not enough rig for the gig' is a crew's blunt verdict on an undersized PA - meant to force the conversation before the show, not explain the disaster after.
Masking doesn't just hide what plays after a loud sound - it can also swallow the instant just before it starts, before your ear catches up.
ADR stands for automatic dialogue replacement, but nothing about it is automatic - skilled, take-by-take re-recording once known by a different name: looping.
Two-voice dubbing covers an entire cast with just two actors - usually one man and one woman splitting every character between them by gender or type.
A marimba's biggest, lowest bars are actually its quietest - the fundamental radiates so inefficiently that engineers add a mic just to keep it from vanishing.
OCT-Surround extends Gunther Theile's three-mic front array to full 5.1 just by adding two more cardioids facing backward, one for each rear channel.
Haunted attractions plant one speaker at the exact spot a scare should come from - listeners always localize to the nearest source, so the trick just works.
Words aren't the only thing a good dub carries over - paralinguistic transfer keeps the original tone, pace and breathiness alive so the emotion survives.
Cymbal sizzle is the shimmering buzz added by rivets or a loose chain laid on the surface, stretching a plain crash into a long, sparkling rattle.
RAI is a stereo miking trick named after the Italian broadcaster that invented it: two mics splayed 100 degrees apart, capsules 21 cm apart.
A speaker's output measured at hundreds of angles forms a sphere of data nicknamed a balloon - software then fills the gaps between the measured points.
